destination.title: Behind the $9 billion promise was a machine that failed

short15: One drop of blood, every test, a nine-billion-dollar company.
Its founder was hailed as the next Steve Jobs.
Then whistleblowers said the device didn't work as advertised.
Many tests secretly ran on other machines, the finger-prick results unreliable, as investors poured in hundreds of millions.
In 2022, a jury convicted the founder of defrauding investors.
Not failure, but intent: knowingly selling a lie.
A bold promise becomes a crime when the deception is deliberate.
Watch the full story on the channel.

candidate_payload_lines: It begins in 2003, with a nineteen-year-old who drops out of Stanford to start a company.
At its peak, around 2014, Theranos was valued at roughly nine billion dollars, briefly making Holmes a paper billionaire and one of the most celebrated founders in America .
In 2015, someone finally asked it in print.

In 2018, the Securities and Exchange Commission charged Holmes with fraud, and she settled those civil charges without admitting or denying wrongdoing — paying a penalty and accepting a ban from leading a public company .
On January 3rd, 2022, the jury delivered a verdict — and it was not a simple one.
It is tempting to read the patient acquittals as a verdict that the technology was fine, or that no one was hurt.
As for Holmes: in November 2022, she was sentenced to about eleven years and three months in federal prison .

shorts.angle: The jury convicted her on four counts, acquitted her on the patient counts, and could not agree on three more.
shorts.type: B - the split verdict, and what an acquittal does and does not mean
shorts.avoids: short15 says only that a jury convicted the founder of defrauding investors. It never mentions the acquittals, the mistrial counts, or the separate trial that came out completely differently.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: If the machine gave patients wrong answers, why did those charges not stick to her?

lines.text: On January 3rd, 2022, the jury delivered a verdict. It was not a simple one.
source_lines: On January 3rd, 2022, the jury delivered a verdict — and it was not a simple one.

lines.text: It convicted her on four counts of fraud against investors. One count of conspiracy, and three counts of wire fraud.
source_lines: It convicted Holmes on four counts of fraud against investors: one count of conspiracy, and three counts of wire fraud, for deceiving specific investors who had put in large sums

lines.text: But on the counts that accused her of defrauding patients, the jury found her not guilty. And on three more investor counts the jurors could not agree, so the judge declared a mistrial.
source_lines: But on the counts that accused her of defrauding patients, the jury found her not guilty.
And on three more investor counts, the jurors could not agree at all, so the judge declared a mistrial on those

lines.text: That is not a finding that the technology was fine, or that no one was hurt. It means only that the prosecution did not prove those charges beyond a reasonable doubt.
source_lines: It is tempting to read the patient acquittals as a verdict that the technology was fine, or that no one was hurt.
An acquittal means only that the prosecution did not prove those particular charges beyond a reasonable doubt — the highest bar in law — not that the underlying conduct was harmless

lines.text: Criminal fraud requires intent to deceive. Proof that someone knowingly made false statements to get something of value.
source_lines: Criminal fraud requires intent to deceive — proof that a person knowingly made false statements to get something of value from someone who relied on them.

lines.text: Prosecutors said she knew about the device's failures and hid them. Her defense said she believed the technology would work.
source_lines: Prosecutors argued that Holmes knew about the device's failures and hid them, pointing to internal results and warnings she had received.
Her defense argued that she was a true believer who genuinely thought the technology would work, and that being wrong is not the same as lying.

lines.text: In November 2022, on those four counts, she was sentenced to about eleven years and three months in federal prison.
source_lines: in November 2022, she was sentenced to about eleven years and three months in federal prison

lines.text: The company's former president was tried separately and convicted on all twelve counts, including the patient counts. Same company. Two different verdicts.

shorts.angle: The board of household names was not oversight. It was the reason nobody looked.
shorts.type: A - why the warning took twelve years to arrive
shorts.avoids: short15 summarises the device, the whistleblowers and the conviction. It never asks the prior question: why hundreds of millions went in before a single person checked whether the machine worked.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: When somebody finally did look, what did they find inside the machine?

lines.text: A beautiful enough story can make very smart people stop asking the most basic question. Does the thing actually work?
source_lines: And a beautiful enough story can make very smart people stop asking the most basic question: does the thing actually work?

lines.text: Its board filled with famous names. Former statesmen and military leaders. It struck a deal with a national pharmacy chain to put its testing in some stores.
source_lines: Its board filled with famous names — former statesmen and military leaders.
It struck a deal with the pharmacy chain Walgreens to put its testing in some stores

lines.text: A board of household names made the company look unimpeachable. A soaring valuation made skeptics look foolish for doubting.
source_lines: A board of household names made the company look unimpeachable; a soaring valuation made skeptics look foolish for doubting.

lines.text: Each famous believer became a reason for the next person not to look too closely. At its peak, around 2014, Theranos was valued at roughly nine billion dollars.
source_lines: Each famous believer became a reason for the next person not to look too closely.
At its peak, around 2014, Theranos was valued at roughly nine billion dollars

lines.text: A blood test then meant a needle, a vial, a lab, a wait. Theranos promised to erase all of that.
source_lines: Today, a blood test means a needle, a vial, a lab, a wait.
Holmes promised to erase all of that.

lines.text: Its device, the Edison, was said to run hundreds of tests from a single painless drop of blood.
source_lines: Her company, Theranos, said its device — called the Edison — could run hundreds of tests from a single, painless drop of blood from your finger, quickly and cheaply

lines.text: A failed app costs money. A blood test that gives the wrong answer can cost someone a diagnosis.
source_lines: A failed app costs you money. A blood test that gives the wrong answer can cost you a diagnosis.

lines.text: For years, with nine billion dollars riding on it, the question went unasked in public. In 2015 a reporter with internal documents asked it in print.
